name: Hyrum's Law
statement: With enough users of an API, every observable behaviour of your system will be depended on by somebody — whatever the contract says.
meaning: Once a system has many users, its written contract stops being the real boundary. Anything users can observe about how it behaves — not just what you documented — becomes something someone relies on, so any change to observable behaviour can break them.
mechanism: At scale, users do not restrict themselves to promised behaviour; deliberately or by accident they build on whatever they can detect — an incidental ordering, a timing characteristic, a side effect, the exact text of an output. Each such reliance quietly turns an implementation detail into a de facto contract. With enough users, the probability that every observable behaviour is depended on by somebody approaches certainty — which is why changing an internal detail can break distant, unknown consumers.

examples.text: A map or set happens to return elements in a particular, never-promised order. Users come to depend on it, so changing the hash implementation — a change no contract forbids — breaks them.
Callers implicitly rely on an operation being 'fast enough'. An optimisation that changes its latency — even one that speeds it up — can break code that depended on the old timing.
Consumers parse the human-readable text of an error message to branch their logic. Rewording it, though the structured contract is untouched, silently breaks them.

The archetype is XKCD 1172: a changelog boasts 'the CPU no longer overheats when you hold down the spacebar', and a user complains it breaks their workflow — they held the spacebar for warmth. Any observable side effect, however absurd, is someone's interface.

whyItMatters: It is the core reason large-scale refactoring is hard: at sufficient scale there is no such thing as a safe, invisible change, because your real interface is everything users can see, not what you wrote down. It reframes API design and deprecation around managing implicit dependencies rather than pretending they don't exist.

working.lead: Treat observable behaviour as the contract
working.text: assume anything users can detect is load-bearing; the documented spec is a floor on your obligations, not a ceiling.
deliberately vary what you don't want depended on — shuffle unspecified iteration order, jitter timings — so no accidental contract can form.
measure real usage, provide migration paths, and move callers before removing behaviour, rather than assuming a spec-legal change is safe.

limits: It is an asymptotic, probabilistic claim: it needs 'a sufficient number of users'. For a small or private API, few incidental dependencies form and the law barely bites. It also does not mean you can never change anything — only that change must be managed through measurement, deprecation policy, staged rollouts, and tooling that fixes callers. And 'all observable behaviours' is a deliberately absolute, rhetorical phrasing of a strong tendency, not a quantified law.
misreadings: It is not a counsel of despair that forbids all change, nor a claim that every tiny API has hidden dependents. It says that at scale your effective interface is wider than your documented one, so changes need to be driven by real usage data and safe migration, not by what the spec technically permits.
origin: Named after Hyrum Wright, a software engineer at Google, whose colleague Titus Winters gave the observation its name. It was popularised through the 2020 O'Reilly book Software Engineering at Google (edited by Winters, Manshreck and Wright) and the single-page site hyrumslaw.com. The exact year Wright first stated it is not firmly documented.

sources.text: Wright, H. & Winters, T. "Hyrum's Law." hyrumslaw.com. — the canonical statement and attribution.
Winters, T., Manshreck, T. & Wright, H. (eds.) (2020). Software Engineering at Google. O'Reilly. — the source that popularised the law.
Munroe, R. "Workflow." xkcd #1172. — the 'spacebar heating' archetype of a depended-upon side effect.
